hook: A government borrows heavily to pay for a new program. Months later a small manufacturer finds that the loan for its new production line costs more than it did a year ago, and it puts the project off. Nobody told the firm to stop investing; the government simply became a big new borrower in the same market for saving.

prereq.q: On the loanable funds graph, what does government borrowing to cover a deficit do?
options: It shifts the demand for loanable funds right
It shifts the supply of loanable funds right
It shifts the money supply left
It moves the economy along the supply curve only
prereq.why: The government is an extra borrower, so demand for loanable funds rises.

prereq.q: A government's outlays exceed its tax revenue this year. What does it do?
options: It borrows the difference, adding to the national debt
It repays part of the national debt
prereq.why: A deficit is financed by borrowing, which adds to the debt.

figure.caption: Government borrowing shifts the demand for loanable funds right; the real interest rate rises and private investment falls.

chain.cause: The government runs a deficit and borrows
chain.effect: the demand for loanable funds shifts right
private investment and interest-sensitive consumption fall
part of the rise in AD from the deficit spending is offset

chain.cause: Investment stays lower year after year
chain.effect: the capital stock and potential output grow more slowly

ideas: Crowding out: government borrowing raises the real interest rate, and private investment falls.

Draw it on the loanable funds graph: Real interest rate (vertical), Quantity of loanable funds (horizontal); government borrowing shifts DLF right (or, in another view, lower public saving shifts SLF left). Either way the real rate rises.
In the short run crowding out shrinks the AD effect of deficit spending. In the long run it leaves a smaller capital stock, so potential output grows more slowly.
Crowding out is largest near full employment and smallest in a deep recession, when private borrowing is weak.

misconception.wrong: Deficit spending lowers the real interest rate, because the government puts money into the economy.
misconception.right: To spend more than it collects, the government borrows. That adds to the demand for loanable funds, so the real interest rate rises and private investment falls.

summary: When a government borrows to pay for a deficit, the demand for loanable funds rises and the real interest rate rises. Private investment and other interest-sensitive spending fall, offsetting part of the boost to AD. Year after year, lower investment means a smaller capital stock and slower growth of potential output. Crowding out is strongest near full employment and is eased by more private saving.
